articles.title: He Walked Into the Fire First
articles.dek: When Los Angeles firefighters lost their own homes while saving their neighbors', it was easy to miss how closely it mirrors something the writer of Hebrews insists about Jesus.
articles.quote: His capacity to help you is not in spite of what he went through — it's built out of it.
articles.body:
In January 2025, wind-driven fires tore through the hills above Los Angeles, and within hours entire neighborhoods in Altadena and Pacific Palisades were gone. Among the firefighters working the line were men and women who lived in those very neighborhoods. Several of them stayed at their stations and on the hoses while the fire moved toward their own streets, because the houses in front of them needed defending too. Some learned only after their shift ended, driving home through smoke still hanging in the air, that their own house had burned while they were busy saving someone else's.

Fire is not an abstract idea to most Filipinos. Ask anyone who has watched an informal settlement go up in an afternoon, or who has stood at a safe distance while neighbors ran back in for a photo album or a sleeping child. What makes the Los Angeles story remarkable is not that firefighters fought a fire. It's that some of them fought it from inside the very loss they were trying to prevent for others. They did not direct the rescue from a radio in a cool, safe command post. They stood in the same heat, breathed the same smoke, and lost what their neighbors lost.

That image is a surprisingly good door into one of the richest passages in the New Testament: Hebrews 2:1-18.

The letter to the Hebrews opens with a warning. The writer is talking to believers who are tired, drifting, tempted to let their faith slide the way a boat slides off its mooring in a current. "We must pay the most careful attention, therefore, to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away" (Hebrews 2:1). Then, almost without warning, the argument turns into something close to poetry. The writer quotes Psalm 8 — "what is mankind that you are mindful of them... You made them a little lower than the angels... and put everything under their feet" (Hebrews 2:6-8) — and then admits the obvious problem: that's not what we actually see. We don't see humanity ruling over everything. We see sickness, failure, death, smallness.

"But we do see Jesus," the writer says, "who was made lower than the angels for a little while, now crowned with glory and honor because he suffered death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone" (Hebrews 2:9).

Read that slowly. Jesus didn't observe human suffering from a safe distance and then wave a hand to fix it. He was "made lower than the angels" — he stepped down out of glory into the very condition he came to rescue people from. The writer calls him "the pioneer of their salvation" (Hebrews 2:10), a word that in Greek, archegos, means something like trailblazer — the one who goes first through a path so others can follow behind him. A pioneer doesn't point at the fire from outside it. A pioneer walks in first.

Then comes a line that should stop every reader in their tracks: "Both the one who makes people holy and those who are made holy are of the same family. So Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers and sisters" (Hebrews 2:11). Not ashamed. Think about what that admits — that there would be reason for shame, that a glorious God associating himself with ordinary, failing, frightened human beings is, by any normal measure, beneath him. And he does it anyway, gladly, the way a man who could have driven straight home chooses instead to stay on someone else's street while his own is burning.

The passage keeps going, and it gets even more specific. "Since the children have flesh and blood, he too shared in their humanity so that by his death he might break the power of him who holds the power of death — that is, the devil — and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death" (Hebrews 2:14-15). Fear of death as slavery — that's a striking diagnosis. Long before the final moment ever arrives, the fear of it quietly runs our lives: how we guard our health, our comfort, our reputations, our grip on everything we think keeps us safe. Jesus didn't deliver us from that fear with a lecture. He walked into death itself, flesh and blood like ours, and came out the other side.

Here is the line that holds the whole chapter together:

"For this reason he had to be made like them, fully human in every way, in order that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in service to God, and that he might make atonement for the sins of the people. Because he himself suffered when he was tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted." (Hebrews 2:17-18, NIV)

Notice the logic. It isn't "even though he suffered, he can still help." It's "because he suffered, he is able to help." His capacity to help you is not in spite of what he went through — it's built out of it. The Greek word for "able" here, dynatai, carries the sense of having the actual power to do something, not just the willingness. Hebrews is saying that Jesus's power to help a tempted, frightened, grieving person comes directly from the fact that he has stood exactly where that person is standing.

It's worth asking why that detail matters so much to the writer. A God who ruled from a distance could still love us. He could still answer prayers, still forgive sins, still promise heaven. But there is something a God like that could never offer: the specific comfort of being understood from the inside. When you are afraid, you don't only want someone with the power to fix it. You want someone who knows what the fear actually feels like in your chest. That is exactly what Hebrews 2 claims Jesus has. Not sympathy observed from the balcony. Shared experience, earned in the fire.

This changes what prayer can feel like. You are not radioing instructions to a commander stationed safely outside the blaze, hoping he understands the danger well enough to send the right help. You are speaking to someone who has already walked that exact kind of smoke, who knows the particular weight of temptation and grief and dying, because he carried it himself, in a body like yours, on a night that was not abstract to him either.

So here is something to keep, the next time you feel like you're facing your trial alone. Hebrews says plainly that Jesus "is not ashamed" to call you family (Hebrews 2:11). Not ashamed of your fear, your weakness, your unfinished faith, your smallness next to the size of what's burning. He stepped down into it first, as the pioneer, so that whatever fire you're standing in right now, you are not standing in it without someone who already knows exactly how hot it is — and who is both willing and able, because of what it cost him, to walk out of it with you.

articles.title: The Fortress That Couldn't See Itself
articles.dek: Edom trusted the cliffs they lived in to keep them safe forever. A strange medical condition shows how easily confidence can make any of us certain we're fine when we're not.
articles.quote: It's rarely our obvious failures that blind us — it's our strengths, the things we've never thought to question.
articles.body:
In 1914, a French neurologist named Joseph Babinski described something so strange that doctors at first assumed the patients were lying. Stroke survivors with a paralyzed left arm would look him in the eye and insist both arms worked perfectly. Ask them to clap, and they'd clap — one hand slicing through the air, the other lying motionless in their lap, utterly ignored. They weren't being difficult. They sincerely believed it. Babinski named the condition anosognosia: the brain's inability to recognize its own deficit.

Decades of research since have only deepened the mystery. The part of the brain that monitors how am I doing is often the very part damaged by the stroke, so the mind has no internal flag to raise. It isn't denial in the ordinary sense. It's a sincere, wired-in blindness. Some of the most striking breakthroughs happen when a patient is finally shown video of themselves failing to move the arm. Seeing it from outside, on a screen, can get through in a way that pleading, arguing, or even their own eyes in a mirror cannot.

Centuries before anyone named anosognosia, the prophet Jeremiah was describing the same blindness in a nation. Edom, the descendants of Esau, lived tucked into the red sandstone canyons of what is now southern Jordan — the same breathtaking terrain where the ancient city of Petra would later be carved. Their capital was reachable only through narrow slot canyons. Their homes were cut into cliff faces hundreds of feet up. For generations, Edom had one great comfort: nobody could touch them up there.

Jeremiah's oracle against Edom opens with a strange, almost gentle question: "Is there no longer wisdom in Teman? Has counsel perished from the prudent? Has their wisdom decayed?" (Jeremiah 49:7). Teman was Edom's byword for shrewdness — a nation famous, even among its enemies, for producing wise men. And yet here they are, about to be undone by a danger they refuse to see coming.

Then comes the verse that names exactly what anosognosia names in a hospital ward — not a stroke this time, but something just as real:

"The terror you inspire and the pride of your heart have deceived you, you who live in the clefts of the rock, who occupy the heights of the hill. Though you build your nest as high as the eagle's, from there I will bring you down," declares the LORD. (Jeremiah 49:16)

Notice what's doing the deceiving. Not weakness. Not ignorance. The very things Edom was proudest of — their fearsome reputation and the impossible height of their homes — are named as the source of the blindness. It's worth sitting with that for a moment, because it's rarely our obvious failures that blind us. It's our strengths. The thing that has always worked for us is the last thing we think to question.

That's what makes pride such a strange disguise. It doesn't feel like pride from the inside. It feels like confidence, like competence, like simply being realistic about how secure you are. Edom didn't think, we are too proud to see our danger. They thought, we live in the rocks, nobody has ever reached us here, we'll be fine. The eagle doesn't build at that height out of arrogance — it builds there because nothing can reach a nest that high. Edom had taken a perfectly reasonable strategy and quietly let it become their god.

Here's the detail easy to miss in a chapter full of judgment. Right in the middle of pronouncing Edom's downfall, God makes an almost tender offer: "Leave your orphans; I will protect their lives. Your widows too can depend on me" (Jeremiah 49:11). This line doesn't fit the tone around it, and that's exactly the point. Even while confronting a nation's pride, God is already making room for the ones who had no part in building that pride — the children, the widows, the people who simply lived in the shadow of someone else's false security. Judgment on the fortress is not judgment on everyone inside it. The vulnerable get a promise of their own.

Put those two verses together and you get something close to real wisdom about relationships and self-understanding. None of us build cliffside homes, but all of us build something — a reputation, a role, a way of coping, a skill we've leaned on so long we stopped questioning it. And the strange thing about that kind of confidence is that it rarely announces itself as pride. It feels like maturity. It feels like having finally figured life out. We say, this is just who I am, in the same breath we might say, this is where I'm blind.

This is where the mirror — or the video screen — matters. Anosognosia patients don't heal by being told harder or louder that something's wrong. They heal when someone finds a way to let them see it for themselves, gently, from outside their own certainty. The people who love us well do the same thing. A friend who says, carefully, can I show you something you might not be seeing, isn't attacking the fortress. They're holding up the mirror. The wisdom of Teman wasn't the problem. Refusing anyone the chance to check it was.

So here's something worth doing this week. Name one place in your life where you feel most secure — a relationship, a skill, a role, a habit of being the strong one — and ask a person who loves you honestly whether it's as solid as it feels from the inside. Not to tear it down. Just to look at it together, the way a doctor finally gets through to a patient by letting them watch themselves on a screen instead of arguing face to face.

And if what gets uncovered is more fragile than you hoped, remember the line God tucked into the middle of Edom's hardest chapter. He doesn't abandon the ones who get caught in the fallout of someone else's false confidence. He says, plainly, leave them with me. The heights we build can be brought down. The people we love while we build them never have to fall with the walls.

articles.title: The Bible With No Pages
articles.dek: In places where owning a Bible can cost you everything, believers have found a way to keep it that no raid can touch — and a young poet discovered the same trick three thousand years earlier.
articles.quote: He didn't hide God's word to keep it secret. He hid it to keep it safe — stored where no circumstance could ever take it from him.
articles.illustration: North Korean underground church Bible memorization
articles.body:
In parts of North Korea, owning a Bible is not a quiet hobby. It is a crime that can send a whole family to a labor camp. So for decades, underground believers there have done something that sounds almost impossible: when a single smuggled Bible reaches a village, someone carefully tears it apart, page by page. Each page goes to a different believer. Overnight, by candlelight or under a blanket with a dim flashlight, that person memorizes every word on their page — then passes it to the next house before sunrise. One page becomes two. Two become a chapter. Eventually an entire book of Scripture exists nowhere on paper. It exists only in dozens of scattered memories, waiting to be spoken aloud again when the believers can safely gather.

If the police raid the house, they find nothing. There is no page to confiscate, no book to burn. The word has already moved somewhere they cannot reach — inside a person.

An ocean away and nearly three thousand years earlier, a young man stumbled onto the very same strategy, not because the law demanded it, but because he chose it. Psalm 119:9–16 opens with a question every parent and every young person eventually asks: "How can a young person stay on the path of purity?" (v.9). The answer isn't willpower. It isn't a list of rules taped to the mirror. It's this: "by living according to your word."

Then the psalmist tells us exactly how he did it. He sought God with his whole heart, refusing to wander from his commands (v.10). He hid God's word so deep inside himself that sin would have to go through it to reach him. He praised God out loud, rehearsing every law he'd been taught (vv.12–13). He found more joy in following God's statutes than in striking it rich (v.14). He meditated on God's precepts the way you'd turn a coin over in your pocket, considering every angle (v.15). And he made a quiet vow: he would delight in God's decrees and would not forget this word (v.16).

But it's verse 11 that carries the weight of the whole passage.

"I have hidden your word in my heart that I might not sin against you." — Psalm 119:11 (NIV)

Here's what's easy to miss on a quick read: the word hidden in Hebrew doesn't mean secretive, like something shameful tucked away. It's the same word used for storing up treasure, or stockpiling grain before a famine, or keeping seed safe for next season's planting. The psalmist wasn't concealing God's word. He was storing it — the way you'd store supplies before a storm you know is coming.

And that's the detail that connects a young Israelite writing poetry to a believer in North Korea tearing pages out of a smuggled Bible. Neither of them memorized Scripture because they happened to enjoy it that day. They did it because they knew a moment was coming when they would have nothing else — no book in hand, no app on a phone, no pastor nearby, no time to look anything up. Only what was already inside them.

The North Korean church does this out of necessity. The psalmist did it by choice, long before the crisis ever arrived. That's the real insight hiding in this passage: he wasn't reacting to temptation. He was preparing for it — treasuring up truth in advance, the way you'd fill a lamp with oil before the sun goes down, not after the dark has already caught you by surprise.

Most of us will never face a raid for owning a Bible. But we all face moments when the word isn't within reach. The argument that flares up faster than you can grab your phone. The 3 a.m. worry with no Wi-Fi to search for comfort. The hospital waiting room where your hands are too shaky to scroll. The decision at work that has to be made in the next ten seconds, long before you could ever look up what's right. In those moments, the only Bible you have is the one you've already stored inside you.

So here's something worth doing this week, in the spirit of the psalmist and in solidarity with believers who have no other choice: pick one verse — maybe this one, maybe another that has quietly steadied you before — and actually memorize it. Not skim it. Not screenshot it. Carry it the slow way: say it over coffee, say it in traffic, say it before you sleep, until it stops being something you read and becomes something you own.

Nobody can confiscate what's hidden in your heart. Not a storm, not a dead battery, not a hard season, not even a prison cell. Store it now, while the storing is easy — so it's already there, waiting, on the day you need it most.

articles.title: The Notebook Behind the Counter
articles.dek: A battered notebook behind a sari-sari store counter holds a quiet secret about the kind of listening God never stops doing.
articles.quote: Mercy isn't a debt we settle once. It's a door we keep leaving open, because ours was left open for us.
articles.body:
Behind the counter of almost every sari-sari store in the Philippines, tucked between the softdrinks and the shampoo sachets, there is usually a notebook. It's cheap, spiral-bound, the cover soft from years of handling. Store owners call it the listahan — the list. Inside are names, dates, small amounts: forty pesos for rice, fifteen for sugar, five for a single stick of cigarette. It is, in effect, a running record of debts owed by neighbors who didn't have enough that day.

Any store owner will tell you the listahan rarely balances. Some names never get paid off. A few people move away owing hundreds of pesos nobody will ever collect. And yet most sari-sari stores keep the notebook anyway. They keep extending the line. They keep writing down the names of people who come back embarrassed, murmuring, "Pautang muna, bukas babayaran" — credit for now, I'll pay tomorrow. Few businesses on earth run this way. It survives because somewhere in the Filipino bones is a stubborn instinct: you don't turn away a neighbor who is asking, because they are hungry today.

That instinct — older than any economics textbook — is exactly what King Solomon is pointing at in a verse easy to read right past.

Proverbs 21 is a burst of short, sharp sayings about justice, bribery, and the two roads a life can take. Verse 12 opens with a warning: the Righteous One — God himself — takes note of the house of the wicked and brings them to ruin. Verse 14 notes how a gift given quietly can calm a furious man. Verse 15 says justice brings joy to the righteous but terror to the wicked. Verse 16 warns that straying from the path of understanding ends in the company of the dead. Tucked right in the middle of all that is this:

"Whoever shuts their ears to the cry of the poor will also cry out and not be answered." (Proverbs 21:13, NIV)

Read it twice and you'll notice something easy to miss the first time through: the same cry shows up on both ends of the sentence. Someone cries out. Someone else shuts their ears. And then, later, that same someone who shut their ears will also cry out — and find no one listening back.

It's worth asking why Solomon built the proverb this way instead of just saying, "Help the poor, or God will punish you." He didn't write a threat. He wrote a mirror. The posture you take toward someone else's need doesn't just affect them — it shapes you. Ears that practice not-hearing don't stay sharp for long. A heart that trains itself to walk past a cry eventually forgets how to recognize one, even its own. Solomon isn't describing an angry God waiting to even the score. He's describing how mercy and deafness both compound over time, the way a muscle either strengthens or atrophies depending on what you ask it to do.

But here's where the proverb opens into something larger than good advice — it opens into the gospel.

Every one of us has, at some point, cried out and desperately needed someone to hear. We have knocked on a door needing mercy we hadn't earned and couldn't repay. And the staggering claim running through the whole Bible is that God, who had every right to shut his ears to that cry, didn't. "The Lord is near to all who call on him... he hears their cry and saves them" (Psalm 145:18–19). In the Gospels, Jesus stopped for a blind beggar named Bartimaeus shouting by the roadside, even when the crowd told the man to be quiet (Mark 10:46–52). He said that whatever we do for the hungry, the stranger, the overlooked, we do for him (Matthew 25:40). The ears that never close belong first to God. Our mercy toward the poor isn't the price of admission for being heard ourselves. It's the overflow of a mercy we already received.

So who is crying out near you today? It's rarely dramatic. It's the text you've been meaning to answer. The coworker who keeps asking for five minutes you keep not giving. The relative with the same request for the third month running, the one you've quietly started tuning out because you're tired of hearing it. It is remarkably easy to build good reasons for not listening. Proverbs doesn't ask you to fix every need that crosses your path — that was never within anyone's power. It asks something smaller and harder: stay a person whose ears still open, even when the debt won't ever be repaid, even when it's inconvenient.

That's what the listahan really is, underneath the arithmetic. It isn't smart business. Nobody keeps a ledger like that for the margins. It's open ears, written down in ballpoint pen, one name at a time.

Mercy isn't a debt we settle once. It's a door we keep leaving open, because ours was left open for us.

Maybe today you can't solve the whole situation in front of you. Few of us ever can. But you can still write the name down. You can still look up when someone calls. Keep your own notebook open — because the God who heard your cry is still listening for the sound of you doing the same for someone else.
